paper_title: Back to Pixels: Lifting Latent Video Diffusion into Pixel Space

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Frontier video generation models work in a VAE latent space that compresses video in both space and time. This compression made training tractable, but now limits high-resolution, controllable, and interactive generation -- doubling resolution quadruples token count, conditions apply to groups of frames rather than individual ones, and each response must wait for the rest of its multi-frame block. We present PixVid, a simple yet effective method that lifts a pretrained latent video model to directly generate every frame in pixel space. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer and replaces the VAE decoder with a convolutional head that renders its outputs into pixels. We find that predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with a larger noise shift, is key to quality. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within $\sim 1.3$M training clips. Working framewise in pixels, it generates at $2\times$ higher resolution with the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned video editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame. Project page: https://chenshuo20.github.io/PixVid/

sections.content: Frontier video generation models work in VAE latent space that compresses video in both space and time. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer and replaces the VAE decoder with convolutional head that renders its outputs into pixels. We find that predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with larger noise shift, is key to quality. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within 1.3M training clips. Working framewise in pixels, it generates at 2 higher resolution with the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned video editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame. Project page: https://chenshuo20.github.io/ PixVid/ 1. Introduction Early video diffusion models [30, 32] generated videos in their native form, as sequences of pixel frames. As models scaled up, the field made two shifts away from pixel space: The first followed latent diffusion [72], moving generation 1 into the latent space of pretrained variational autoencoder (VAE) [48], initially with one latent per frame [6, 7]. The second extended the compression to time, using 3D VAEs to merge every few frames into single latent that corresponds to no individual frame [85, 93]. For generating short clips offline at moderate resolution, this was favorable trade: compression made training tractable at scale, at the cost of frozen VAE that ruled out end-to-end training and capped quality at its reconstruction [14, 23, 77]. Video generation models have since outgrown this setting: they now power real-time interactive world models [27, 33, 79] through causal few-step distillation [38, 97], and serve as geometry-conditioned renderers for editing and games [43, 62, 63]. Yet these systems inherit the VAEs fixed compression in space and time, which works against each new demand. Under real-time compute budget, doubling the resolution yields 4 more tokens and 16 more attention compute, while cutting tokens requires more aggressive VAE that further reduces quality. Precise editing requires conditions aligned to individual frames, but when several frames share one latent, fast motion blurs and objects deform  (Fig. 5)  . Temporal compression also limits responsiveness. Since common latent world models [27, 37, 38, 79, 92, 97] autoregressively generate frames in blocks, the frame corresponding to control cannot be generated until all controls for the full block are received. This results in minimum control-to-screen latency proportional to the block size, barrier that no model-side optimization can remove. These limitations motivate removing the VAE altogether and generating every frame directly as pixels, which naively would bring back the token counts and training costs that latent models avoid. Recent pixel-space image models overcome both challenges [13, 18, 19, 41, 50, 98] by modeling semantics over large pixel patches [50] and delegating fine details to lightweight decoder [19], thus keeping the token count and training cost reasonable. Moreover, although training video models from scratch demands prohibitive data and compute resources, pretrained latent model already captures high-level semantics and dynamics. Hence, finetuning it into pixel space video model only requires changing the output interface, which is more feasible task. In this work, we present PixVid, recipe that lifts pretrained latent video diffusion model into frame-wise pixelspace model, in which every token covers 1 patch of exactly one frame, so no condition or action spans multiple frames. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer (DiT) and replaces both the encoder and the decoder from the VAE  (Fig. 2)  . At input, patch embedding that initializes from the VAE encoder allows the DiT to start training from close to its pretrained latent distribution. At output, lightweight detailer head renders the DiT tokens into pixels; it is convolutional to suppress the patch-grid artifacts of linear head [88], and causal in time to allow autoregressive generation. We further identify the following key techniques: 1) predicting clean video (x-prediction) rather than velocity, since velocity prediction forces the network to model full-rank per-pixel noise [50]; 2) using larger noise shift, since redundant pixels retain more signal at the same noise level; and 3) using the Euler sampler, since pixel color values are numerically sensitive to higher order solvers like UniPC [101]. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B [85], PixVid converges within 1.3M training clips sampled from 64K videos, or about 4K B200 GPU-hours. It achieves competitive quality with the original latent model on VBench [39], and the recipe transfers across Wan2.1 and Wan2.2-based models with different VAEs. Generating frame by frame in pixels, it introduces several benefits, as shown in Fig. 1. Resolution: doubling the patch size lets PixVid generate 960 1664 with the same number of tokens per frame as at 480 832. Control: with the same control branch as the latent model, depth-conditioned editing keeps 98% of the sources fast motion, versus 83% for an identically finetuned latent model. Latency: after autoregressive distillation, each camera control takes effect at the next frame rather than the next block, cutting median latency from 495 ms to 34 ms while still streaming in real time. To summarize, our main contributions are as follows: We propose PixVid, recipe that lifts pretrained latent video diffusion model into frame-wise pixel-space model, converging quickly to competitive quality. We identify the design choices that make this lift work: causal convolutional detailer head with 9 fewer patch seams than linear head, x-prediction with 80 less pixel noise than v-prediction, and larger noise shift than the latent model. We show frame-wise pixel generation overcomes three structural limitations of latent models: resolution scaling, control alignment under fast motion, and control-toscreen latency. 2. Related Work Pixel-Space Diffusion. Latent diffusion [7, 68, 72] has been favored for efficient training using spatial and temporal compression for video [8, 85, 93], at the price of VAE reconstruction bottleneck. Pixel-space diffusion models for images [22, 29, 46, 78] and videos [5, 30, 32, 76] bypass VAE but become costly at high resolution, historically requiring cascaded or multi-resolution designs [20, 26, 31, 71, 74, 81]. Recent methods improved pixel-space image generation, training from scratch [13, 15, 19, 34, 35, 50, 55, 57, 58, 61, 87, 98] or finetuning from latent checkpoints to make training tenable [13, 18, 41]. Pixel-space video generation is less explored. Concurrent works train from scratch, and they either focus on smaller class-conditioned 2 benchmarks [84] or have undesirable patch artifacts [88]. We finetune pretrained latent video model, inheriting its prior capabilities and maintaining competitive quality. Controllable Video Generation and Editing. Early video editors applied image diffusion models with heuristics such as cross-frame shared self-attention [24, 47, 70, 89] or propagated edits [4, 67, 91]. Video diffusion models improve consistency and robustness, with recent models producing precise, aligned edits and structure-guided generation [10, 25, 43, 45, 49, 62, 73, 94]. Interactive Video Generation. Interactive generation produces frames as stream, typically with autoregressive video diffusion models [11, 12, 21, 80, 90]. Combined with few-step distillation [17, 38, 92, 9597, 104], latent world models respond to user actions across diverse scenes in real time [27, 33, 60, 79], but temporal compression delays each action, e.g. by up to three frames for Wans four-frame latents [85]. Per-frame latent [9, 83] and pixel-space [2, 65] world models avoid this delay but are trained from scratch on single genre. PixVid is finetuned from general pretrained model and responds to actions at the next frame. 3. Methods Our goal is to generate every frame directly in pixels without training pixel-space video model from scratch, while removing the VAE bottleneck. PixVid achieves this by lifting pretrained latent video diffusion model into framewise pixel-space model, as shown in Fig. 2. We describe its architecture in Sec. 3.1 and how we train it from the latent model in Sec. 3.2, including key design choices. We then adapt it to efficient high-resolution generation in Sec. 3.3, precise video editing in Sec. 3.4, and low-latency autoregressive generation in Sec. 3.5. 3.1. Architecture PixVid keeps the DiT [68] backbone of pretrained latent video model and replaces the VAE: linear patch embedding maps pixels to tokens, and lightweight convolutional detailer head renders the DiT outputs directly into pixels. Frame-Wise Tokenization. Latent video models merge several frames into one latent [85, 93], so conditions apply to groups of frames. PixVid instead gives each frame its own tokens, each covering 1 pixel patch. Conditions then align with individual frames, and an autoregressive model can respond to actions at the next frame. Although this approach uses more tokens per clip than with temporal compression, the spatial token count does not grow with resolution as it is determined by the adjustable patch size rather than frozen VAE. Detailer Head. Since the DiT captures global structure and leaves only local details to render, we implement the detailer as lightweight 3D convolutional decoder, sharing this insight with pixel-space image models [18, 19, 41]. Unlike their U-Net detailers, which also encode the noisy pixels of each patch, ours keeps only the decoder path and reads only the DiT tokens. It stacks = log2 up blocks, each upsampling by 1 2 2, so the head maps each token to 1 pixel patch and predicts the clean video. Its convolutions also run across neighboring tokens rather than within each patch, which largely suppresses checkerboard artifacts at token boundaries. They are causal in time, so the detailer models local temporal structure without reading future frames and supports frame-by-frame generation. See App. A.2 for details. 3.2. Training from Latent Model PixVid finetunes end-to-end in pixel space from pretrained latent model, with initialized DiT and input patchification, x-prediction, larger noise shift, and auxiliary losses. Initialization. To retain the pretrained latent models prior, we inherit its DiT weights and randomly initialize the detailer head. Following AsymFlow [13], we approximate the VAE encoder with linear map fitted offline between pixel patches and their latents, and compose it with the pretrained patch embedding to initialize the pixel patch embedding. We further employ an internal timestep calibration, with scale estimated alongside A, to ensure the signalto-noise ratios of latent and pixel spaces are aligned. The DiT thus initially receives inputs close to the latents it was trained on. Full details appear in App. A.1. x-Prediction. Efficient High-Resolution Generation The high-level semantic content of video changes little with resolution, so higher resolution should mainly require finer rendering, not more tokens. latent DiT cannot exploit this, as doubling the resolution yields 4 more latent tokens. PixVid instead doubles the patch size from to 2p and adds one up block to the detailer, keeping the token grid unchanged  (Fig. 3)  . Unlike PixelDiT [98], whose token count grows with resolution, or DiP [19] and L2P [18], which add no detailer levels, this gives the doubled resolution its own upsampling level without much additional cost. We finetune the patch-2p model from the patch-p model. Its patch embedding fuses 2 2 average pooling with the patch-p embedding, so the DiT initially sees downsampled version of its input, and the new upsampling block starts as an identity pass-through, acting as nearest-neighbor upsampling. We also double both the calibration scale and the noise shift [23], so the DiT sees the same noise schedule as at patch p. See App. A.3 for details. Figure 3. Patch-size adaptation. Precise Video Editing Precise video editing, such as re-rendering video from its per-frame depth, requires the generated video to align with the condition at every frame. Latent models typically encode the condition with the same VAE as the video [43], so several condition frames share one latent, leading to inaccurate alignment, especially in fast motions. In PixVid, the condition is tokenized per frame as the corresponding video, so generation and condition are aligned at the frame level, without changing the conditioning mechanism. Low-Latency Autoregressive Generation Interactive applications stream video in response to user controls, such as camera or motion inputs, and should react to each control as soon as it arrives. An autoregressive model generates video in blocks, and block can start only once the controls for all its frames have arrived. In temporally compressed latent model, each block spans at least one latent, i.e., several frames, so new control waits for the rest of its block, delay that no throughput-side optimization can remove  (Fig. 6)  . PixVid can generate singleframe blocks, so each control takes effect at the next frame. To achieve this, we lift bidirectional latent model to pixel space with the recipe above and distill it into few-step causal model with Self Forcing [38]. The causal detailer decodes one frame at time from cached features of previous frames, keeping its cost per frame constant. Single-frame blocks trade some throughput for this latency gain, which we analyze in Sec. 4.5. 4. Experiments We evaluate PixVid on text-to-video generation in Sec. 4.2, followed by its three applications: efficient high-resolution generation in Sec. 4.3, precise video editing in Sec. 4.4, and low-latency autoregressive generation in Sec. 4.5. Finally, we ablate our key design choices in Sec. 4.6. 4.1. Experimental Setup We lift three pretrained latent models into pixel space: Wan2.1-T2V-14B [85] for text-to-video and high-resolution generation, Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B for video editing and ablations, and the camera-controlled SolarWM-5B [37] for interactive generation. Unless otherwise noted, models generate 21-frame videos with patch size = 16 and sample with 50 Euler steps at the training shift. Each experiment below gives its key setup. Efficient High-Resolution Generation Setup. We generate 960 1664 videos with the same 30 52 token grid per frame as 480832 generation by doubling the patch size from 16 to 32. We first train patch-16 pixel model at 480832, then finetune it at 9601664 with patch 32 with twice the shift and an additional scale-2 calibration. We train on 40K synthetic videos resized and cropped to the training resolution, and evaluate with the same VBench protocol as Sec. 4.2. Results. Using the same number of tokens per frame as 480p, the 960 1664 model reaches the highest VBench total of 85.09 and the best imaging, aesthetic, backgroundconsistency, and temporal-flickering scores in Tab. 1. Its semantic score of 80.68 is below the 480 832 models, mostly in color. Doubling the patch size therefore keeps PixVid competitive at 4 times the pixels per frame. Its cost per clip stays close to latent models at this resolution: 21-frame clip has 32, 760 tokens and takes 192 on one B200, against 37, 440 tokens and 176 for Wan2.1-VAE latent model (App. B.7). Since VBench resizes frames to at most 512 pixels before scoring, it does not measure the added detail, which we show in Fig. 1(a). 4.4. Precise Video Editing Setup. We add the control branch of VACE [43] to PixVid1.3B and finetune it to re-render video from its perframe depth and caption. We compare with VACE-1.3B, finetuned with the same control branch, data, and training settings; and with off-the-shelf depth-conditioned models without finetuning. We train on 79K stock videos with varied camera and object motion and paired depth [16], and evaluate on 1,000 held-out clips across alignment, temporal fidelity, and video quality. Alignment is measured by optical flow error, the fraction of source motion kept, and depth error, while temporal fidelity and video quality are Figure 5. Depth-conditioned Editing. Our pixel model enables precise video editing under high motion, while the temporally compressed latent model morphs and blurs fast-moving objects. measured by temporal LPIPS, FVMD [54], and FVD [82]. Fast clips are the quarter with the most motion; details are in App. B.4. Results. PixVid keeps the scene intact under fast motion, where the latent model morphs and blurs moving objects  (Fig. 5)  . On fast clips, it lowers motion error by 40% and depth error by 20%, and keeps 98% of the source motion, against 83% for the finetuned latent model and at most 63% for the zero-shot models (Tab. 2). It also has the lowest FVMD and tLP and leads on all four per-clip metrics over all 1,000 clips (Tab. 7), while its FVD trails (118 vs. 91). 4.5. Low-Latency Autoregressive Generation Setup. We compare with the official causal student distilled from the same base, referred to as SolarWM, which generates blocks of 12 frames (3 latents). We evaluate quality and camera following on camera paths from nine public datasets, and responsiveness on abrupt turns, measuring how closely the generated motion follows each control (App. B.5). We measure control-to-screen latency, which includes both the wait for controls from the same block and the models generation time. We time both models on one B200 GPU with the same kernels. Results. All ablations finetune Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B for 10K iterations and change one design choice at time from our final recipe: the convolutional head, x-prediction, and shift. The noise shift decides how training and sampling are spread across noise levels, which affects global structure as well as local noise, so we score the shift sweep on VBench, with all 946 prompts and one video per prompt. Conclusion Latent video diffusion models compress video in space and time with VAE. PixVid removes this compression by efficiently finetuning pretrained latent model to generate every frame directly in pixels, reaching quality competitive with the original model. Working frame by frame in pixels, it overcomes three structural limitations of latent models: resolution scaling, control alignment under fast motion, and control-to-screen latency. Limitations and future work. Without temporal compression, PixVid processes 3.9 as many tokens per second of video as Wan2.1 at 480 832, so short low-resolution clips cost more than with latent model, although the gap closes at higher resolution and streaming stays faster than real time (App. B.7). Generating directly in pixels also opens up training options that frozen VAE rules out. Losses and rewards can be defined on pixels, enabling adversarial training and RL with pixel-space rewards. Because all models then share the same output space, distillation across architectures or from mixed teachers also becomes possible. Acknowledgments.
